synopsis: This tutorial organizes world modeling for robotics around two questions: what future representation is predicted, and how that prediction connects to action generation. It separates observation-space prediction from latent, point-track, symbolic, and physical-state prediction, then compares visual-subgoal grounding, predictive-feature conditioning, joint video-action generation, and auxiliary future-prediction training. Its contribution is a conceptual design map rather than a new trained system or empirical benchmark. A central interpretive issue is that its inference-coupled definition of a world action model does not cleanly accommodate its training-only auxiliary category. [e03, e05, e08, e09, e10, e11, e12, e13, e14, e16]

problem.text: The same world-model terminology covers latent dynamics, video generators, simulators, and action-conditioned predictors, although these systems predict different quantities and occupy different roles in a robot. The tutorial seeks a common vocabulary grounded in task-relevant robot–environment states, goal-directed policies, and the distinction between predicting a future and generating actions intended to realize it.

contributions.text: Defines the world to include both robot and environment, and distinguishes a predictive world model from a policy that supplies robot actions.
Organizes observation-space models by observation representation and action abstraction, while organizing state-space models by the structure of their predicted state.
Presents four video-based policy paradigms and argues that their central trade-off concerns how explicitly they represent the future and how tightly they couple it to action prediction.

inputs: For the conceptual world model: current observation o_t and candidate action a_t, whose representation depends on the intended application.
For the video-based policy formulations: current observation o_t and language instruction l.
Observations may include proprioception, RGB or RGB-D images, or point clouds.
outputs: World-model predictions: future observations or task-relevant states, potentially over a trajectory.
Policy predictions: robot actions, with explicit visual futures, predictive features, or training-time future supervision depending on the paradigm.
The tutorial itself outputs definitions and a taxonomy; it does not introduce a runnable policy.

steps.name: Establish the task and system role
steps.detail: Choose the robot, objects, environmental variables, goals, and constraints relevant to the task. A policy maps intent and observation to actions; a world model predicts consequences under conditioning actions. Prediction requires an additional planning, decision-making, or control mechanism to accomplish a physical task.

steps.name: Choose observation prediction and action conditioning
steps.detail: Observation-space models predict RGB, multi-view RGB, RGB-D, or point clouds. The tutorial contrasts spatial explicitness with data availability, including pseudo-depth annotations of ordinary videos. Conditioning ranges across robot commands, interface controls, learned latent actions, and language. Interface control can change viewpoint without modeling robot dynamics; language supplies semantic guidance without specifying precise motor commands.

steps.name: Choose a structured state alternative
steps.detail: Latent models compress observations into learned features. Point-track models retain selected scene motion but introduce a point-selection prior. Neural-symbolic models ground Boolean predicates in perception and model skill preconditions and effects. Physical-state models reconstruct a scene, fit dynamics and rendering parameters against real interactions, and predict through physics equations.

steps.name: Imagine, then ground the future into actions
steps.detail: A video predictor generates future visual subgoals from observation and instruction. A separate inverse dynamics model or goal-conditioned policy converts the current observation and generated future into actions. Intermediate end-effector poses, object poses, or optical flow can assist grounding. Generated subgoal errors can propagate into action errors.

steps.name: Condition action prediction on video features
steps.detail: Extract intermediate spatiotemporal features from a video-model backbone and feed them to an action predictor without decoding a complete future video. The authors motivate this interface through iterative video-sampling costs, while acknowledging that latent features make it harder to determine whether the policy uses meaningful future information.

steps.name: Generate video and actions jointly
steps.detail: Use a single generative model for the joint distribution of future observations and action sequences. A common route extends a pretrained video backbone to produce actions and adapts it using action-labeled robot trajectories. Shared representations are intended to improve consistency, although visual and action objectives may compete.

steps.name: Use future prediction as auxiliary supervision
steps.detail: Add a future-observation prediction branch to a policy during training. Its loss shapes the shared representation alongside action supervision. The branch can be removed at inference, leaving only action prediction; any control benefit then depends on what the auxiliary task transferred into the retained policy.

training.text: The tutorial distinguishes reconstruction-based latent learning, prediction of future embeddings without pixel reconstruction, and state features obtained from pretrained visual or vision-language encoders. Latent-action learning instead infers compact transition variables from action-free videos using reconstruction and an information bottleneck.

Modular visual planning permits separate data sources for video learning and robot-action grounding. Joint video-action adaptation requires action-labeled robot trajectories. Auxiliary policies combine video and action supervision, with loss balancing identified as a potential difficulty.

inference.text: Runtime dependencies distinguish the paradigms: generated visual subgoals feed a grounding module; predictive features feed an action module; joint models generate coupled outputs; auxiliary-only policies may retain no video branch. The tutorial supplies no universal feedback, replanning, or action-chunk execution procedure.

An imagined future or predicted action sequence does not establish successful physical execution. The tutorial explains interfaces intended to bridge prediction and control, but provides no execution measurements with which to assess that bridge.

equations.explanation: The generic world-model formulation conditions on observation o_t and action a_t. The prediction target y_{t+1} is either a future observation ô_{t+1} or state x_{t+1}; θ parameterizes the predictor. The text also permits trajectory targets.

The WAM overview couples future observations and actions over horizon H, given observation and language instruction l. This is a schematic description of coupling; the subsequent paradigms differ in architecture and in whether future observations are decoded at inference.

Imagine-then-execute separates visual planning through p_θ from action grounding through q_ϕ. The generated future becomes an input to inverse dynamics or a goal-conditioned policy, exposing the interface through which prediction errors can affect actions.

limitations.text: There are no original quantitative experiments, benchmark tables, or mechanism ablations in the supplied tutorial. Claims about reduced inference cost, improved consistency, or useful representations are explanatory arguments rather than measured comparative results here.

The definition has an unresolved boundary: Section 1.3 requires inference-time coupling, whereas Section 3 includes auxiliary prediction whose branch can be discarded before inference. Likewise, the output-based VLA comparison is insufficient to distinguish policies that output only actions while using predictive features internally.

Coverage is deliberately concise and focuses the WAM taxonomy on recent video-based robotic policies. Classical model-based control and reinforcement learning enter selectively, so the categories should not be treated as an exhaustive taxonomy of predictive control.

The tutorial explicitly identifies grounding errors, opaque predictive features, scarce action-labeled data, competing joint objectives, and uncertain transfer from auxiliary prediction as paradigm-specific weaknesses. It does not experimentally rank their importance across tasks.

reproduction.text: There is no tutorial-specific experiment to reproduce. Implementing a representative system would require the cited method's architecture, data, objectives, optimization settings, runtime procedure, and evaluation protocol; this paper provides conceptual pathways rather than those specifications.

A useful reader-proposed test would compare an action-only policy with the same policy trained using auxiliary future prediction, holding robot data and evaluation tasks fixed. Measure executed task success and runtime separately from prediction quality. This would test whether predictive supervision benefits control without requiring a full joint generator.
The first page mentions a GitHub page, but repository contents were not supplied or inspected. No code availability, installation success, or reproduced experiment is established by this reading.

reasoning.text: The recorded foundational survey/resource classification fits a tutorial whose output is definitions and an organizing framework. Architecture, prediction paradigm, and quadrant are appropriately Not applicable to this resource: its discussion of separate modules and single generative models does not assign an architecture to the tutorial itself. The WAM-definition tension warrants editorial discussion but does not undermine this resource-level classification.

discussionQuestions: Should training-only future supervision qualify a policy as a WAM, or should inference-time predictive dependence define the boundary? [e03, e14]
What intervention would distinguish useful future information from task-correlated features in a video-conditioned policy? [e12]
How should visual-plan feasibility and action-grounding error be measured separately in imagine-then-execute systems? [e11]

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author block, arXiv version stamp, Abstract, and GitHub-page label
evidence.detail: The title and three authors match the catalog. The supplied artifact identifies arXiv:2607.00836v7, dated 26 August 2026. The abstract describes a concise tutorial rather than an exhaustive survey; a GitHub page is mentioned.

The world includes the robot and task-relevant environment. Tasks specify goals and constraints over world states; policies map human intent and current observation to robot action through potentially different architectures.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section 1.3, definitions, WM/WAM comparison, and taxonomy-scope paragraph
evidence.detail: World models predict observations or states under actions and require an additional control mechanism. WAMs are defined through inference-time coupling of action generation and observation prediction. The taxonomy focuses on recent video-based policies.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 2–3, Section 1.3, paragraph beginning The differences between WAM and VLA
evidence.detail: The tutorial characterizes a typical VLA as a direct observation-and-language-to-action mapping and illustrates the contrast through action-only output versus inclusion of future-observation prediction.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section 2 opening and Section 2.1 opening, unnumbered predictive-distribution equations
evidence.detail: The prediction target y is an observation or state, conditioned on current observation and action. The formulation permits future trajectories and distinguishes observation-space from state-space models.
The text compares RGB, multi-view RGB, RGB-D, and point clouds by spatial information and availability, including estimated monocular depth as a way to construct pseudo-RGB-D data.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 3–4, Section 2.1, Action representation: Robot action, Interface action, Latent action, and Language
evidence.detail: Conditioning spans motor commands, user or viewpoint controls, compact transition variables learned from unlabeled video, and semantic instructions. These choices support different uses, from robot simulation to interactive viewing, pretraining, and visual planning.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Section 2.2 opening and Latent state model
evidence.detail: State-space prediction abstracts observations into compact representations. Latent states may be learned through reconstruction, future-feature prediction, or pretrained encoders and can support reinforcement learning or model-predictive control.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 2.2, Point track model and Neural-symbolic model
evidence.detail: Point tracks provide compact motion representations with a selection prior. Neural-symbolic models use perceptually grounded Boolean predicates and skill preconditions and effects for high-level planning.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 2.2, Physical state model
evidence.detail: Physical models use explicit dynamics variables. The described pipeline reconstructs a scene, fits simulation and rendering parameters using real trajectories, and predicts future states through physics-based transitions.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 3 opening joint-distribution equation and Imagine-then-execute subsection
evidence.detail: The overview couples predicted visual trajectories and actions. Imagine-then-execute generates visual subgoals, then uses inverse dynamics or a goal-conditioned policy to obtain actions; separate data sources and intermediate geometric cues are possible, while subgoal errors can propagate.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 3, Video-feature-conditioned action prediction
evidence.detail: Intermediate video-backbone features condition an action predictor without complete video decoding. Reduced sampling cost is a stated motivation; feature opacity is a limitation. The extracted action-distribution equation lacks its left-hand variable.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Section 3, Joint video-action modeling
evidence.detail: A single generative model represents visual futures and actions jointly. Video-backbone adaptation uses action-labeled robot trajectories; potential consistency benefits are balanced against data scarcity and competing prediction objectives.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section 3, Auxiliary video prediction for policy learning
evidence.detail: A future-prediction branch supplies auxiliary training supervision and can be removed at inference. The authors caution that visual prediction need not improve control and that balancing losses can be difficult.

The synthesis compares modular grounding, latent-feature transparency, joint optimization, and auxiliary representation transfer, framing future explicitness and coupling strength as central design choices.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 1–8, Abstract and complete Sections 1–3; References begin on p. 8 and continue through p. 10
evidence.detail: The supplied paper contains conceptual definitions, model families, equations, and qualitative trade-offs followed by references. It presents no original experimental protocol, quantitative results table, ablation study, or tutorial-specific implementation recipe.
